name: ClickUp
subcategory: team projects, issues and delivery planning
tagline: Combine tasks, docs, goals, dashboards, and simple automations for a small team

tiers.name: Free Forever
tiers.limits: Unlimited tasks/members, 60 MB storage, 5 spaces, 40 lists/space, 100 automation runs/month, 5 active rules, 3 whiteboards, 1 form, 30-day message history

tiers.name: Unlimited
tiers.limits: Unlimited storage/spaces/folders/forms, 1,000 automation runs/month and 500 active automation rules

tiers.name: Business
tiers.limits: 5,000 automation runs/month, unlimited active rules, advanced dashboards/timelines/time tracking and workload

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom seats/security/support and up to 250,000 automation runs/month

pricing.freeTierCaps: Unlimited tasks/members; 60 MB storage, 5 spaces, 40 lists per space, 100 automation runs/month, 5 active rules, 3 whiteboards, 1 form and 30-day message history
pricing.hiddenCosts: AI is not included in the core plan price: ClickUp Brain AI is $9/user/month and Everything AI is $28/user/month, with any annual discount shown separately. Automation usage has hard monthly caps, and Enterprise is required for the highest cap.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For ClickUp, combine tasks, docs, goals, dashboards, and simple automations for a small team. The hard boundary is breadth, integrations, mobile apps, reporting, and a highly configurable workflow engine, plus collaboration, integrations, and organizational trust.
coreLoopDIY: Plan and track team work through tasks, boards, milestones, docs, goals, dashboards, and simple automations, with comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
whatYouLose: breadth, integrations, mobile apps, reporting, and a highly configurable workflow engine
ongoingBurden: auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for ClickUp because teams pay because project state has to remain authoritative through staff changes, outages, and years of accumulated workflow exceptions. The recurring cost buys auth, permissions, notifications, search, migrations, audit history, integrations, backups, and uptime, not just the visible interface.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Plane

rejectedAlternatives.name: YouTrack

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Unlimited plan and a small-team tracker DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for ClickUp in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and Docker Compose; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: plan and track team work through tasks, boards, milestones, docs, goals, dashboards, and simple automations, with comments and a searchable activity history for a small team.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement organizations, projects, members, issues, labels, cycles, and milestones.
Provide list, kanban, and simple timeline views backed by one canonical issue model.
Add comments, mentions, assignments, watchers, and a complete activity log.
Implement project roles for owner, member, and viewer and test every mutation.
Add search, CSV import or export, email notifications, and daily database backups.
Ship Docker Compose, health checks, migrations, seed data, and an admin recovery command.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out hundreds of external integrations.
Deliberately leave out enterprise portfolio planning and SSO.
Deliberately leave out native mobile clients and vendor-operated uptime.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
